newsitem.title: USA: Study finds U.S companies frustrated with insurers.
newsitem.headline: Study finds U.S companies frustrated with insurers.

text.p: A national survey of about 2,000 corporate buyers of insurance found that they were frustrated with their insurers and unhappy with the products and services they receive.

The survey, conducted by the Quality Insurance Congress (QIC) over the last year, showed "there is a significant gap between the system of insurance and customers' expectations," said Jay Deragon, executive director of the QIC in Nashville, Tenn.

The survey, which was the subject of a panel discussion at the Insurance Leadership Forum here, found small, medium and large commercial customers complaining about simple things like confusing bills and more complex issues such as the lack of creative solutions to their risk management problems.
"The reality is the customer wants a few more things," said Scott Lange, director of risk management for Microsoft Corp and one of the session's panelists.
"That's not to say there hasn't been some progress in the industry," he said. "But we think there's quite a ways to go yet."
Lange, a member of the QIC, criticized the insurance industry for failing to respond to customers' needs and for making insurance products more complicated than they need to be.
"We want things to be more simple and every day it seems to get more complex," he said.

He complained about the confusing language in policies, inefficient distribution systems, poor customer service, a lack of customized products as well as the need for multiple products rather than just one.
"We don't want 50 different products," Lange said. "We want one seamless product."
And because of the lack of specialized products, he said insurance buyers have little loyalty to any insurer.
"You've got to be more creative than you've been," he said.
The customers' complaints deliver a "strong wake-up call to the industry," said John E. Cay III, president of Palmer & Cay Inc insurance brokerage in Savannah, Ga.
As an industry, "we just aren't making the grade," said Philip Engel, president of CNA Financial Corp's CNA Insurance in Chicago and a member of QIC.
And the research shows that the insurance industry is falling behind other financial service business in terms of customer satisfaction.
The QIC, which has 400 members, brings insurers, brokers and reinsurers together with their customers to learn how to improve service.
Although the industry is working harder to get better faster, "improvement is not happening fast enough," Deragon said.
And the research sends a "very strong message that quality is important," Engel said.
